note: I started from the consensus centre of about $44-45B (Carr $30-60B, TD Cowen $30-75B), about $0.82 on 160 MHz x 335M pops. Real mid-band prices have fallen since 2015, and roughly $0.20-0.30/MHz-pop of clearing and altimeter costs sit on top of bids, so the all-in price is about lower C-band's in nominal terms (a real decline). I kept the range wide because of the reference class: 5 of the last 8 big US auctions beat consensus (AWS-3 about 3x, C-band 1.7x), while 600 MHz (0.5x) and 2.5 GHz (0.15x) fell well short. On the 335M-pop basis, lower C-band itself was only about $0.87.

This is the price distribution multiplied by 53.6B MHz-pops (160 MHz x 335M). The $78B P90 allows a lower-C-band-style beat of about 1.7x consensus. The $23.5B P10 allows a 600 MHz-style miss of about 0.5x, driven by AT&T's leverage, T-Mobile's build-versus-buy discipline and Verizon's comment that the band takes 4-5 years to deploy.

The likely 2029-30 deals mix new-band auctions (2.7 GHz, the 25 MHz AWS-3-adjacent band, possibly 4.4 GHz) with private sales (EchoStar's remainder, Array's C-band, low-band resales). In the base rate, 2021-22 auctions cleared at $0.67-0.87 and private sales in 2025-26 ran $0.52-2.53, with a median near $1.2. Real mid-band prices have fallen as supply rose (Canada's second tranche cleared 90% lower). So the median slides a little below today's level, and the range is wide because which deals happen will decide the median.

From 2013 to 2024 there were essentially no spectrum-only deals of $5B or more (about 0.2 a year). The 3 in 2025-26 came from one forced seller (EchoStar) and one new buyer (SpaceX). The main candidate for 2027-30 is EchoStar's paired AWS-3 remainder (about $8B on the books, to be sold by Sept 2028), with smaller odds on SpaceX or Amazon buying more, or a Viasat/L-band deal. I modelled the count as roughly Poisson with a mean of about 1.1 and some overdispersion.

Growth decayed from +38% to +20% over 2022-25, and mature markets settle in the high teens (UK +18%, Switzerland 20-25%). Ericsson's North American smartphone forecast is a 13% CAGR, and FWA traffic should grow about 18-20% as line adds slow. The blend gives about 16% a year, or about 330 EB by 2030. The P10 assumes growth drops toward 8-10% (FWA saturation, Wi-Fi). The P90 is close to CTIA's own roughly 22% path, which vendor and industry forecasts have usually overshot.

I extended the 2030 path with growth decaying further to about 9-12% a year over 2031-35, the pattern that every maturing market and Ericsson's own forecast (14% by 2031) show. The range is wide and log-skewed: P10 is about 6% growth after a weak 2030, and P90 is about 16% sustained by uplink-heavy AI and 6G. CTIA- and Nokia-style AI step-change scenarios sit at or above the P90.

The base is 0.06% in 2025. If share doubles each year it reaches about 2% in 2030, and growing 1.5x a year gives about 0.5%. Text and voice AI is light, AI glasses tether through phones and often Wi-Fi, and robotaxis add only about 0.1%. Vendor scenario forecasts (GSMA 5-20%, Nokia's broad definitions) have a record of overshooting. The upper tail reflects the TikTok precedent, a new video-heavy app category reaching double-digit share in about 4 years, and the chance that generative-video apps get counted.

The base is about 19.6M at end-2026. Annual adds have already peaked (3.8M in 2025, 3.6M in 2026, and Verizon's Q3 adds fell 39% year on year). Decaying adds of about 3.1, 2.6, 2.2 and 1.8M give about 29M, close to the carriers' targets (T-Mobile 15M by 2030, Verizon well beyond 8-9M by 2028). New Street's roughly 32M capacity ceiling and product S-curves cap the top. The P10 has adds collapsing as fiber overbuild and higher churn hit.

This is the ratio of my revenue forecast (P50 $264B) to my traffic forecast (P50 328 EB). Revenue per GB falls about 11% a year as traffic growth slows, not the 20% a year of 2020-25, when traffic grew 25-38%. Traffic uncertainty drives most of the range. A naive extension of -20% a year would give about $0.49, which is below my P10.

Upper C-band (160 MHz) is nearly certain under the statute and FCC schedule. The 2.7 GHz band (about 200 MHz, Carr's 2028 target) gets about 57% by 2030, after the usual 1-3 year slip on US mid-band auctions, and the 25 MHz 1675/2020 band about 50%. The P90 needs an upper mid-band (4.4 or 7 GHz) or mmWave auction to finish by 2030, which I put at about 15-25%.

Outside view: statutory spectrum mandates are usually met late or only in part; about 75% of Spectrum Act targets were auctioned within the decade. The 2025 law's 800 MHz pipeline excludes 1,350 MHz of candidate spectrum (3.1-3.45 and 7.4-8.4 GHz), so about 75-80% delivery gives about 630. The 300 MHz FCC minimum is met by upper C-band plus 2.7 GHz (P10). The upper tail adds 7.125-7.4 GHz and part of 4.4-4.94 GHz, with a possible mmWave auction such as upper 37 GHz, which would add a lot of MHz cheaply.

About 79 MHz is pending: EchoStar's 65 MHz (about 83% to close by 2027, about 93% by 2030) and Grain's 14 MHz (about 87% approved). FCC approved every major 2025-26 transfer. SpaceX made about 5 spectrum moves in 13 months, so further buying is plausible: Auction 115 wins (about 37%), EchoStar's paired AWS-3, regional pieces. That fattens the upper tail. Musk's line that the 800 MHz deal is the 'last critical piece' keeps the median near the pending total.

The base is well under $1B, and the whole legacy satellite-phone (MSS) industry earns a few $B a year (Iridium $0.87B). My bottom-up 2030 estimate is $1.5-2.5B of SpaceX wholesale from about 150M monthly users at roughly $1/month, plus possible US retail, AST at $0.5-1.5B, and Apple/Globalstar/Amazon plus IoT at under $1B in total, for about $3-5B. Forecasts for new satellite services have historically overshot, and D2D is mostly bundled at near-zero marginal price. The upper tail is broadband-class D2D monetized at premium tiers.

I put the chance of a direct US launch by 2030 at about 70%, and it depends on the EchoStar closing (Nov 2027) and next-gen satellites, whose timelines usually slip. Reference class for entrants: cable MVNOs, with tens of millions of broadband homes to bundle into, reached about 1M lines in about 1.5 years and about 3M in about 3 years. Dish/Boost never scaled organically. A 2028 launch at a cable-like pace gives about 1-2.5M by end-2030, so the overall median is under 1M with a long right tail.

The 2007-2025 nominal CAGR was about 3% (roughly flat real), and I used 2.4% a year from $235B. The 2026 run-rate is firmer (AT&T wireless service +5%, T-Mobile +6-9%, price increases), and FWA adds about 0.7% a year. Offsetting that, cable takes share with free lines and Verizon's ARPA fell 1.9%. The P10 is about 1% CAGR (a price war after SpaceX enters) and the P90 about 4%. CTIA restating its basis is an extra source of width.

US incumbent telcos have mostly traded at 6-8x, and today's 6.9x is close to the long-run average once T-Mobile's old premium is set aside. Multiples mean-revert, with about ±1.0-1.2x of 4-year dispersion. Downside risks are SpaceX price pressure and a 6G/upper C-band capex cycle around 2030. The upside is a convergence or M&A re-rating.

Cable has added a steady 3-3.6M lines a year in 2022-26 (+3.4M in the 12 months to Q3 2026), and mobile penetration of cable broadband homes is still only about 20%. Adds decaying about 10% a year gives about 35.5M, and a straight-line trend gives about 38.6M. The P10 has adds roughly halving as broadband losses shrink the base, free lines roll off and carriers retaliate on price.

Capex has been flat at $29-30B for 2023-25 after the 2022 peak of $39B, and past cycles troughed 20-30% below peak before the next generation's ramp. 2030 sits at the trough-to-ramp turn: upper C-band deployment in 2029-31 (Verizon says 4-5 years) plus early 6G, with about 2.5% inflation. Against that, AT&T and Verizon have cut capex outlooks and the industry is in harvest mode. The P90 assumes a 2021-22-style spectrum-driven surge.

Once the FCC sets a procedures date, US auctions almost always start on time: Auctions 107, 110, 108 and 103 did, and 105 slipped only a month during COVID. Statutory and Treasury pressure (at least 100 MHz by July 2027) adds to that. Clock and assignment phases for comparable band-plan auctions took 2.5-3 months (107: Dec to Feb; 110: Oct to Jan). An April 27 start therefore implies a close around Aug-Oct 2027, leaving room for slips. The residual risk is litigation, FAA/altimeter interference or a long bidding war.

This is consistent with my price distribution. $0.94 on the 335M basis means proceeds of at least about $50.4B, which sits around the 62nd-63rd percentile of my conditional distribution (median $0.82). That gives about 38%, times about 96% that bidding concludes by 2028, or about 36%. The reference class of consensus beats (C-band, AWS-3) keeps this from being lower, and real price declines plus heavy add-on costs keep it below 50%.

SpaceX was engaged in the Auction 115 rulemaking, asking that satellite coverage count toward buildout (denied) and seeking satellite or SCS access to the band. It won licences in the 2026 AWS-3 re-auction, possibly as a warm-up, and has huge balance-sheet capacity and stated telco ambitions. Against that, the FCC denied satellite buildout credit, Musk called 800 MHz the last critical piece, and a 4 GHz band needs a terrestrial grid SpaceX lacks. I put about 55% on SpaceX qualifying and about 65-70% on it winning something if it does.

The FCC approved the transfer in May 2026, the licences are already in trust, and SpaceX's funding of EchoStar interest through November 2027 points to a contractual close around Nov 30, 2027. Approved deals with set dates usually close on schedule. But the target is only one month before the deadline, and the Dish subsidiaries are in Chapter 11, so a modest slip past 31 Dec is the main risk.

The FCC approved every major 2025-26 spectrum transfer, with conditions, in about 6-12 months; SpaceX-EchoStar took about 8. SpaceX holds no low-band, so the spectrum screen is not an issue, and the Carr FCC has been accommodating to SpaceX. The application was accepted on Nov 10, 2026, leaving about 13 months against a 180-day informal shot clock. The residual risk is AT&T/Verizon opposition, 800 MHz public-safety interference issues or delays from added conditions.

This needs the EchoStar closing (about Nov 2027) plus either next-gen D2D satellites on AWS-4 (launches from 2027, expanded service targeted for end-2027) or a terrestrial grid for 800 MHz. All of that has to happen within about 13 months of closing. SpaceX has the billing base and the stated intent. But new-entrant and new-constellation timelines (Dish 5G, AST, Kuiper, Starship) usually slip 6-12 months, which puts the median launch near end-2028.

Beating the fourth-largest operator (Comcast or Charter at roughly 18-25M by 2035) needs about 20M directly billed US subscribers. Cable did about 24M in about 9 years with tens of millions of bundled broadband homes. Dish/Boost never scaled organically, and satellites cannot carry dense-urban demand. The probability is mostly an organic SpaceX success tail plus about a 3-4% chance it buys a carrier or a cable mobile base.

The US base rate for a non-telecom tech company buying a facilities-based carrier is essentially zero over 30 years; Google Fi and others stayed MVNOs. SpaceX's stated telco ambitions, its need for towers and a core network, and the fact that a small regional carrier would count raise this above the base rate. Cable mobile businesses are core to the broadband bundle and unlikely to be sold.

For revenue per GB to rise, traffic growth would have to fall below revenue growth of about 2-4%. CTIA's lowest growth since 2010 was +14% (2020), and my central path stays at 13-18% through 2030. Year-to-year noise of about ±6 points gives under 6% across the four years. A CTIA methodology break (for example, splitting out FWA) or a sharp FWA pullback adds a few points.

The central path has growth at 14-18% for 2027-30. But CTIA's series is noisy, with re-accelerations of 12 points or more in 2018, 2021 and 2022 driven by unlimited plans, FWA and methodology. Per-year odds of topping 25% (about 3-12%), partly correlated across years, give about 19%. That is slightly above the research digest's 15% because of the series' history of jumps.

Spec freeze to first US commercial launch was about 9-13 months for 5G (AT&T's hotspot in Dec 2018, Verizon in April 2019) and about 21 months for LTE. Release 21's ASN.1 freeze in March 2029 therefore points to a first launch between Dec 2029 and late 2030, right at the deadline. T-Mobile says it will be first around 2030, and US policy favours a race. Against that are possible 3GPP schedule slips, no new 6G band by 2030, weak carrier ROI, and a strict Release 21 test that rules out rebranded 5G-Advanced.

Candidates are 7.125-7.4 GHz (NTIA report due Dec 2026) and part of 4.4-4.94 GHz (DoD relocation plans under review). Federal-band study-to-auction has ranged from 14 months (3.45 GHz, with a strong push) to about 10 years (CBRS), and mid-band auctions usually slip 1-3 years. The 2.7 GHz band alone could largely satisfy the 200 MHz July-2029 federal tranche, which reduces pressure to rush 7 GHz before WRC-27 takes effect in 2029.

EchoStar is a motivated seller with a stated target to sell its remaining licences (about $8.45B on its books, mainly paired AWS-3) by Sept 2028, and it has executed every sale so far. I give that about 60% within the window, allowing for slippage and piecemeal sales. Array still holds C-band facing buildout milestones (about 30%), Anterix is in a strategic review after the band was widened (about 22%), and NextNav depends on FCC action (about 8%). Treated as roughly independent, that gives about 75%.

In most rolling 4-year windows since 2010, an equal-weight basket of T, VZ and TMUS has trailed the S&P 500. It mostly won in bear-market windows such as 2000-03 and 2007-10. A low starting multiple (about 6.9x), about 5-6% dividend yields and a richly valued, AI-heavy S&P argue for some mean reversion. SpaceX entry, cable share gains and a capex cycle around 2030 are structural headwinds.

Next-cheapest-capacity bound: carriers paid about $0.9-1.2 for 3.45 GHz they could use at once (AT&T-EchoStar $22.65B less about $11-13B for the 600 MHz part, over 30 MHz x 335M). Upper C-band carries about $0.30/MHz-pop of add-on costs ($16B / 53.6B MHz-pops) and a 4-5 year deployment lag (a 15-20% discount), so carrier-only bidding clears near $0.55-0.75. 3.45 GHz (2022) cleared at about 75% of the C-band price, consistent with that. I modelled a mixture: 55% no serious SpaceX bidding (median $0.65) and 45% SpaceX bids hard (median $0.95), which gives P10/P50/P90 of about 0.47/0.77/1.29.

Proceeds = 160 MHz x 335M pops x price = 53.6B MHz-pops x my price quantiles (0.45/0.77/1.30), giving about $24B/$41B/$70B. This sits inside TD Cowen's $30-75B and centres near Carr's $30-60B midpoint. I kept a fat right tail because analysts badly underestimated the 2021 auction ($81B vs $40-52B) and Verizon still pays up (88% of Auction 113 at $2.53/MHz-pop).

The median depends on which deals happen in 2029-30. Mid-band FCC auctions that slip into that window (2.7 GHz, 4.4 GHz, 1.6 GHz) should clear at about $0.3-0.7, given about 35% more mid-band supply by then and traffic growing only about 15%. Private sales over $1B (low-band, paired AWS, C-band remainders) run about $1.2-2.5. With 1-4 qualifying deals, two auctions plus one private sale gives a median near $0.6, and the reverse mix gives about $1.3-1.5. The result is a wide, slightly bimodal range centred near $0.86.

Candidate-by-candidate: a $5B+ sale of EchoStar's remaining licences (book $8.45B, paired AWS-3 marked at $8.1B, sale targeted by Sept 2028), about 50%; another SpaceX purchase about 20%; Amazon about 10%; a carrier swap or sale about 10%; Anterix, NextNav or Ligado about 10%; other about 10%. That gives an expected count of about 1.1 and P(0) of about 26%. The 2013-24 base rate was roughly 0.2 a year; the 2025-26 burst came from EchoStar's forced exit.

Bottom-up for 2030: phones 335M x about 37 GB/month (10%/yr from 25 GB, below Ericsson's 13%, which has overshot before) x 12 = about 149 EB. FWA about 28.5M average lines x about 520 GB/month (7%/yr from about 371 GB implied in 2025) x 12 = about 178 EB. Other devices add about 10 EB, for about 337 EB. Top-down, growth decaying from 18% to 11% gives about 310 EB. The P90 sits on CTIA's 4x-by-2032 path (22% CAGR, about 430 EB); the P10 assumes FWA adds stall and phone growth is about 7%.

From about 333 EB in 2030, growth of 8-10%/yr gives about 500-540. Bottom-up 2035: phones 340M x about 60 GB x 12 = 245 EB, FWA about 30M x about 750 GB x 12 = 270 EB, plus vehicles, robots and glasses about 20 EB, for about 535 EB. Low case: FWA shrinks to about 22M lines under fiber overbuild and phones reach 48 GB, about 350 EB. High case: AI uplink, 7 GHz capacity and 38M FWA lines at 1 TB, about 880 EB. Log-wide range.

From 0.06% in Apr 2025: if GenAI app traffic grows 120%/yr against total traffic at about 18%/yr, the share is 0.06% x 51.5 / 2.29, about 1.35%. Adding the pieces: voice and vision assistants about 0.5 GB/month per phone (about 1.2% of phone traffic), AI-video generation apps about 0.3-1%, 60K robotaxis x 20 GB/day = 0.44 EB (about 0.13%), and tethered glasses about 0.05%. Total about 1.5-2.5%. The upper tail is fat because vendors measure generously and AI-video apps are hard to classify; the downside comes from AI features folded into OS and apps where they are not counted.

Start from about 20M at end-2026 (19M in Q3). Net adds decay from 3.6M (2026) by about 12%/yr: 3.2 + 2.8 + 2.4 + 2.1 = about +10.5M, so about 30M. That matches company targets: T-Mobile 15M by 2030, Verizon 'well beyond' 8-9M, AT&T about 5M. The downside (adds fall 30%/yr, then churn and fiber substitution) gives about 25M; the upside (adds hold, upper C-band capacity) about 35M, near New Street's 32M headroom estimate. T-Mobile no longer discloses its count, which adds resolution noise.

Ratio of my own forecasts: service revenue P50 $266B / traffic P50 333 EB = $0.80/GB, against $1.48 in 2025 (about -11.6%/yr, a slower decline than the -20%/yr since 2020 because traffic growth is slowing). Combining log-uncertainty (traffic sd about 0.18, revenue about 0.06, correlation 0.3) gives about $0.63-0.98.

Auction by auction, with a common FCC-pace factor in a Monte Carlo: upper C-band 160 MHz (97%); 2.7 GHz 100-210 MHz (70%; Carr targets 2028, typical slip 1-3 years); 1.6/2.0 GHz 20-25 MHz (62%); 7.125-7.4 GHz 275 MHz (42%; on Carr's end-2028 slate, NTIA report due Dec 2026); a 4.4 GHz portion (18%); mmWave (4%; no plan found). The simulation gives a lump at 160 (about 25%), a median of about 395, and P90 about 750-800. I shaded the tail down slightly.

Same model to 2035: 2.7 GHz 88%, 7 GHz 75%, a 4.4-4.94 GHz portion of 100-300 MHz 50%, 1.3 GHz 25%, plus small chances of mmWave (about 12-15%) or a reversal at upper 6 GHz. The median is about 160+180+22+275 plus a coin-flip 4.4 GHz tranche, about 685. That is about 85% of the 800 MHz statutory pipeline, close to the base rate that 75% of Spectrum Act targets were met within a decade. The P10 is a DoD-resistance or political-slowdown world (UCB plus 2.7 GHz only); the P90 adds a mmWave or upper-6 GHz award.

Monte Carlo: EchoStar 65 MHz (92% closed by 2030) + Grain 800 MHz 12-14 MHz (88%) + tiny AWS-3 wins. Add-ons: Auction 115 wins (48%; 30% of those only token, otherwise median 35 MHz pop-weighted), 2.7 GHz wins (20% x about 30 MHz), a secondary purchase (20% x 5-25 MHz) and a 2020-2025 MHz adjacency (30% x 5). That gives about 69/89/139. The median sits above the 79 MHz pending because at least one substantive addition is more likely than not.

Sum of operators for 2030. SpaceX wholesale from carrier partners (about 50-80M entitled subscribers at $1-5/month) plus US direct retail, about $2.5B. AST revenue share about $1.2B (from $150-200M in 2026 with about 100 satellites by 2028). Apple and Amazon-Globalstar about $0.5B; China (Tiantong and others) about $0.5B; IoT (Skylo, Iridium NTN) about $0.5B; total about $5B. The low case is bundling at near-zero price (about $2B); the high case is broadband-class next-gen D2D priced as a $5-10 add-on (about $13-15B). For scale, the whole legacy MSS industry is a few $B.

Lines = P(launch) x ramp. I put about a 50% chance of a direct plan on owned spectrum by end-2028 (FT: SpaceX told investors it plans a US consumer service; owned spectrum arrives at the Nov 2027 EchoStar closing) and about 20% of no direct plan by 2030. Conditional on a 2028 launch: about 5M US Starlink broadband homes x 30% attach x about 1.6 lines, plus about 1M rural switchers, gives about 2.5-3M by 2030. Analogs are slow: DISH/Boost about 7M after 5 years mostly by acquisition, cable 24M in about 8 years on 60M broadband homes.

Lines x ARPU: phone lines about +1%/yr, ARPU about +1%/yr, plus FWA (about 3M adds/yr x $50 x 12, about $1.8B/yr or about +0.75%/yr), gives about 2.5-3%/yr. $235B x 1.025^5 = $266B. The P10 is Analysys Mason's near-flat view (+0.6%/yr, about $242B) with SpaceX and cable price pressure; the P90 is T-Mobile-style ARPA gains in a 3-network market (+4%/yr, about $286B). 2007-25 nominal CAGR was 3.0%.

Starting from about 6.9x (T 6.7, VZ 6.7, TMUS 7.4), incumbents have mostly traded at 6-8x. Scenario weights: grind 50% (6.5-7.5x), price pressure from SpaceX and cable 30% (5-6x), convergence or M&A premium 20% (8x+). A 6G and upper C-band capex cycle around 2030 limits re-rating, while T-Mobile's lost premium could partly return. The weighted median is about 6.85x.

Start from 24.1M in Q3 2026 (about 25M at end-2026), with recent adds about 3.3-3.4M/yr (Charter +1.8M, Comcast +1.6M over 12 months). With adds decaying about 10%/yr (3.0 + 2.7 + 2.4 + 2.1), I get about 35M. Faster decay plus broadband losses (Q3: -144K Comcast, -233K Charter) and SpaceX pressure gives about 31M; Cox integration and steady adds give about 38-39M. The attach ceiling on about 60M broadband homes x about 1.7 lines is far above these levels.

Base: harvest-mode capex flat at about $29-30B nominal (2023-25), about $30-31B by 2030. Add upper C-band deployment from about 2029-31 ($2-4B/yr, smaller than the 2022 C-band spike of about +$9B over trend) and early 6G or 7 GHz builds. Low case: network sharing, capex shifting to fiber, AT&T's lowered outlook, about $26-27B. High case: full 6G, UCB and AI-uplink densification plus any SpaceX terrestrial build, near the $39B 2022 peak.

Bidding starts 27 Apr 2027 (short-forms due Jan 2027), with a statutory deadline of 4 Jul 2027. Comparable clock-plus-assignment auctions took about 10 weeks (Auction 107) and about 13 weeks (Auction 110), so the auction should close by about Aug 2027 with four months to spare. The residual risk is a slip of 5+ months (shutdown, aviation or satellite litigation, IT problems).

Taken from my price distribution: median $0.77, P90 $1.30. P(price > $0.94 | auction concluded) is about 31%, times P(concluded by 2028) of about 0.95, about 30%. Most of that probability comes from the about 45% scenario in which SpaceX bids hard (about 50% above $0.94 there) against about 14% without it.

SpaceX lobbied on the Auction 115 rules (it sought satellite buildout credit, which the FCC deferred), bid in Auction 113 (2 of 6 licences won, read as a practice run), and analysts expect it to be a major bidder. Musk's stated approach is to buy spectrum and build. I estimate P(applies and qualifies) about 68% x P(wins at least one of 3,248 licences) about 75% x P(concludes by 2028) 0.95, about 48%. Without satellite buildout credit it needs a terrestrial plan, which tempers this.

The FCC approved the transfer in May 2026, the licences have been in trust since 22 May 2026, and closing is targeted for about 30 Nov 2027, leaving only a one-month buffer before the deadline. The search found no creditor challenge aimed specifically at the SpaceX closing, but the Dish DBS and Dish Wireless Chapter 11 cases and the Hughes bondholder suits add tail risk. Contracted closing dates usually hold; I allow about 19% for slippage into 2028 or a renegotiation.

The filing was accepted 10 Nov 2026. The FCC's 180-day informal clock points to about mid-2027, and SpaceX-EchoStar took about 8 months under Carr, leaving about 13 months of runway. SpaceX holds no other low-band, so there are no spectrum-screen issues, and T-Mobile shares in Grain's resale gain, which dulls incumbent opposition. Residual risk comes from interference conditions on 800 MHz satellite use or a political or DOJ delay.

The FT reports SpaceX told investors it plans a US consumer mobile service, and Shotwell wants a full telco. Owned spectrum usable only arrives at the about Nov 2027 EchoStar closing, leaving about 13 months to launch. Handset support for AWS-4 or the next-gen D2D bands and the lack of any Big 3 MVNO are the binding constraints. A satellite-only or bundled plan billed by SpaceX would also count, which helps.

The fourth-largest of the five would be Charter at about 20-25M lines in 2035. My 2030 SpaceX median is about 1M direct subscribers, so it would need roughly 4x/yr growth or a carrier acquisition. Cable took about 8 years to reach 24M with 60M broadband homes to sell into. Paths are a cheap satellite-plus-terrestrial bundle that scales, or buying a carrier or cable mobile base (included at about 5%).

Light Reading reports Musk's approach as 'won't buy a telco, will build one'. The Big 3 are effectively unbuyable (scale, DT control of TMUS), and cable mobile is tied to the broadband bundle. The remaining paths are SpaceX or Amazon buying a small regional facilities-based carrier for sites and customers (about 8%), a cable mobile carve-out (about 3%), or a larger surprise (about 4%).

Revenue per GB rises only if traffic growth falls below revenue growth (about 2-3%) in some year. CTIA traffic growth has not been below about 14% since at least 2010, and my 2030 paths have growth of about 9-15%. The residual comes mostly from a CTIA methodology or restatement artefact or a traffic plateau from FWA reversal.

Growth fell from 32% to 20% in 2025 and FWA adds are slowing, so a year above 25% needs a new load driver. Upper C-band capacity arrives about 2029-31 (Verizon says 4-5 years to deploy). The precedent is 2020-22, when FWA plus C-band lifted growth from 14% to 38%, so it is possible: a CTIA definitional change or an AI or FWA surge could do it in one year.

The Rel-21 ASN.1 freeze is set for Mar 2029. The first US LTE launch came about 21 months after its ASN.1 freeze and 3GPP 5G about 13 months after, which points to Apr-Dec 2030, right at the deadline. There is political pressure for US 6G leadership, Ericsson expects first systems in 2030, and a token paid FWA launch would count. Against that: flat capex, weak carrier ROI, little competitive marketing pressure, and possible 3GPP schedule slip.

Carr aims to finish 7 GHz, 1.6 GHz and 2.7 GHz auctions by end-2028, though Commissioner Gomez doubts it, and NTIA's 7.125-7.4 GHz report is due Dec 2026. US mid-band auctions have usually slipped 1-3 years, which still leaves about a 42% chance for 7 GHz by end-2030. A 4.4-4.94 GHz auction (NTIA targets an auction by 2030) adds about 18%, correlated, for about 47% that either happens. This matches the CDF of my 2030 MHz forecast.

Union of four candidates. EchoStar's remaining licences: a motivated seller targeting completion by Sept 2028, with Verizon and SpaceX as known suitors, about 60%. Array's retained C-band about 35%, Anterix (strategic review, 10 MHz at 900 MHz) about 25%, NextNav (contingent on the FCC's 900 MHz decision) about 15%. Independence gives about 83%; I discount for correlated buyer appetite and for the 'most of its spectrum' wording.

Equal-weight carriers' expected return is about a 4.2% average yield plus about 3% growth and buybacks, about 7%/yr, against a richly valued, AI-heavy S&P with about 5-7% expected. The carriers have already de-rated on the SpaceX threat (TMUS about -22% YTD). Against that, the historical base rate for carriers beating the S&P over 4-year windows is about 30-35%, and SpaceX competition and a 2030 capex cycle are further headwinds. Tracking error of about 20%/yr makes the outcome close to a coin flip, tilted to No.

This is gross proceeds divided by 53.6B MHz-pops (160 MHz x 335M), so the figures are the proceeds forecast divided through. On the same 335M-pop basis the lower C-band works out to about $0.87, and the follow-on 3.45 GHz tranche cleared about 25% below it. I tilt up from that reference class because SpaceX is a plausible new aggressive bidder, in the role DISH played in AWS-3 in 2015, when proceeds ran 2-4x consensus. The carriers also have a reason to bid defensively after losing 9-13% of their value on 9 Oct. The tilt is capped by about $16B of add-on costs (about $0.30/MHz-pop, double the lower C-band's) and by AT&T and Verizon's leverage.

I modelled this as a mixture. In the roughly 40% of cases where SpaceX does not bid seriously, the median is about $38B. In the roughly 60% where it does, the median is about $52B. Both use a log spread of about 0.42, reflecting how far past US auctions landed from consensus (AWS-3 and lower C-band far above, 600 MHz and 2.5 GHz far below). My median sits at the top of the internal researchers' $30-45B and near the middle of Carr's $30-60B and TD Cowen's $30-75B. Press reports that SpaceX may bid aggressively ('Elon is coming') support the upper tail, while the ~$16B add-on and altimeter costs and slower traffic growth support the lower one.

The likely 2029-30 deals mix cheap auction supply with expensive private sales. On the auction side: 2.7 GHz (about 210 MHz with radar constraints, around $0.3-0.8), possibly 7 GHz (around $0.1-0.3) and 1675/2020 MHz (around $0.5-1.5). On the private side: low-band and paired sales at $1.2-2.0, where sub-1 GHz is scarce and SpaceX and Amazon are now buyers. With only a few deals in the sample, the median depends heavily on which deals happen, so the range is wide. The centre is near the 2025-26 comparables of about $1.0-1.4, shaded down for new supply.

I summed rough per-candidate probabilities to an expected count of about 1.4. EchoStar's paired AWS-3, marked at about $8B, must be sold by Sept 2028 (about 50% that it goes as a single deal of $5B or more in the window). I give about 30% to further SpaceX buying, about 13% to Amazon buying terrestrial spectrum, about 17% to carrier swaps or post-auction trades, and smaller shares to takeovers where spectrum is most of the value and to intermediary flips. A Poisson-like count with mean 1.4 gives a median of 1 and a P90 of about 3. That is far above the pre-2025 base rate of about 0.2 a year, because new deep-pocketed buyers now exist, but there are few large nationwide sellers left.

I built this bottom-up. Phones grow about 11% a year from 98 EB, which is what the 2024-25 split implies once FWA is taken out. FWA grows from about 13.7M to about 28M average lines, with per-line use rising about 5% a year. Together that gives about 325-340 EB in 2030, with annual growth falling from about 19% to 12%. The upper tail (about 22% CAGR) covers Ericsson's mid-2026 re-acceleration led by North America, upper C-band capacity feeding FWA, and uplink-heavy AI. The lower tail covers FWA saturating at about 25M lines and phone growth falling below 10%.

I extended the 2030 distribution at about 9-12% a year after 2030, consistent with mature markets settling in the high teens and still decelerating. The upper tail allows for Nokia's AI-driven scenario (about 4x 2026 levels by 2035, roughly 16% CAGR) and 6G or 7 GHz capacity. The lower tail allows for saturation at about 7% a year from a weak 2030. The internal research's 520 (325-930) and CTIA's 4x-by-2032 path bracket this range.

The starting point is 0.06% (Ericsson, April 2025). Reaching 3% by 2030 requires AI traffic to grow about 120% a year in absolute terms, which is plausible with multimodal camera assistants, AI glasses, GenAI video apps (likely counted under Ericsson-style app measurement) and robotaxi uplink. Ericsson's medium uplink scenario (3x uplink by 2031) implies about 10% AI share, and GSMA Intelligence says 5-20%. I discount those vendor scenarios for their history of overshooting, for Wi-Fi offload, and for AI features being absorbed into existing apps where they are not measured separately. The resolution also uses a vendor measurement, which leans toward a higher figure.

I start from about 19.5-20M at end-2026 and add decaying net adds of 3.2, 2.9, 2.6 and 2.3M, giving about 31M. Faster decay gives about 28M. The company targets (T-Mobile 15M by 2030, Verizon 'well beyond' 8-9M, AT&T about 5M) sum to about 30M, inside New Street's estimate of about 32M Big 3 capacity. Upper C-band deployment adds headroom. The downside is that a mobile capacity squeeze, the very thing the spectrum thesis predicts, would lead carriers to ration FWA.

This is the ratio of my service revenue and traffic forecasts: median $266B divided by median 335 EB is about $0.79, roughly -12% a year from $1.48. That is a slower decline than the -20% a year since 2020, because traffic growth is slowing. The P10 combines low revenue with high traffic, and the P90 combines high revenue with low traffic. The result matches the research's $0.53-1.07 range.

Upper C-band (160 MHz) is about 95% likely to finish bidding by 2030. 2.7 GHz (about 210 MHz, Carr targets 2028, and it plausibly fills the statutory 200 MHz federal tranche due for auction by July 2029) is about 55-60% likely, allowing for the usual 1-3 year US slippage. 1675-1695 plus 2020-2025 (25 MHz) is about 55%, and 7.125-7.4 GHz (275 MHz) about 24%. So the P10 is upper C-band alone, the P50 is upper C-band plus most of 2.7 GHz, and the P90 needs every band on time.

OBBBA sets an 800 MHz pipeline, at least 300 MHz to be auctioned by 2034, and auction authority to Sept 2034. That gives a strong fiscal and legal push, helped by WRC-27 identification of 7 GHz and 4.4 GHz and by demand for 6G. Applying the roughly 75% completion rate of the 2012 Spectrum Act targets to 800 MHz gives about 600-650. The lower tail reflects Defense Department resistance, the excluded 3.1-3.45 and 7.4-8.4 GHz bands, and political change after 2028.

The base is about 79 MHz: EchoStar's 65 (FCC-approved, in trust, closing Nov 2027, about 92% by 2030) plus Grain's 14 (about 88%). I add small regional AWS-3 holdings (Tristar, Auction 113) and a roughly 40% chance of some Auction 115 wins, worth perhaps 10-40 MHz nationwide-equivalent. The upper tail covers SpaceX buying EchoStar's paired AWS-3 (about 8 MHz equivalent), 2020-2025 MHz next to AWS-4, or 2.7 GHz. SpaceX added about 79 MHz in 13 months, so further buying is credible, but Musk called 800 MHz the 'last critical piece'.

I summed by operator for 2030. Starlink Mobile could have about 100-200M monthly users at low wholesale ARPU (about $2-4B), plus a SpaceX US retail plan. AST's wholesale revenue share with AT&T, Verizon and Vodafone could be about $1-3B, Apple's payments to Globalstar/Amazon a few hundred million, and Skylo, Iridium NTN and IoT add more. The whole legacy MSS industry is only a few billion dollars a year, and satellite service is often bundled at near-zero price, which bounds the downside. A long right tail is warranted because broadband-class next-generation D2D starts in 2027-28.

I put about a 75% chance on a SpaceX-billed US plan by 2030. If it launches in 2028-29, a bundle with Starlink broadband plus a satellite or 800 MHz offer could reach about 1-3M by end-2030. Reference classes: DISH/Boost reached about 7M only with acquired bases, and cable MVNOs took 7-8 years to reach about 24M. The upper tail allows for an acquisition (for example Boost or a regional carrier) or a cheap satellite-plus-terrestrial plan that goes viral. The roughly 25% chance of no meaningful launch puts the P10 near zero.

I use the CTIA-basis $235B for 2025 and the 2007-2025 nominal CAGR of about 3%, which gives about $272B. I shade that slightly for Verizon's ARPA decline, cable free lines and SpaceX entry. On the upside, AT&T's wireless service revenue grew 5% and T-Mobile's 6-9% in 2026, FWA adds about $10B of revenue by 2030, and price increases and satellite or AI tiers add more. The range of 1-4% annual growth is the 2007-2025 record of steady low-single-digit growth.

US incumbent carriers have mostly traded at 6-8x. The research weights its 2030 scenarios at 50% grind (6-7.5x), 30% price pressure (5-6x) and 20% convergence premium (8x or more), which centres near today's 6.9x. The bull upside is spectrum monetised through M&A or a SpaceX or hyperscaler bid. The downside is SpaceX and cable competition and a 6G capex cycle around 2030.

The base is 24.1M at Q3 2026, adding about 3.4M a year. A linear path gives about 38.6M by end-2030, and adds decaying 10-15% a year give about 33-36M. Comcast's adds are already slowing (368k against 414k a year earlier), and shrinking cable broadband bases cap how many mobile lines can be attached. Free-line promotions and Cox inside Charter support continued growth.

Capex has been flat at about $29-30B since 2023, against a 5G peak of $39B in 2022. Past generations peaked early and then fell 20-30%. In 2030 the industry is near the turn from trough to ramp: upper C-band deployment in 2028-30, early 6G or 7 GHz overlays, and inflation of about 2.5% a year push it up. Capital-light strategies, AT&T's lower long-term guidance and T-Mobile's roughly $10B push it down. A capacity crunch (the bull case) would lift the upper tail toward the 2022 peak.

Bidding is scheduled to start 27 April 2027, under a statutory July 2027 deadline. Recent clock auctions ran about 2.5-3 months including the assignment phase (Auction 107 about 2.5 months, Auction 110 about 3, Auction 97 about 2.5), which points to a close around Aug-Sept 2027 with several months of slack. The residual risk is a start-date slip (altimeter or FAA disputes, cable earth-station objections, litigation or a government shutdown) of more than about five months.

The $0.94 threshold equals $50.4B of gross bids (0.94 x 160 x 335M). That sits at about the 63rd percentile of my proceeds distribution (median $44B, log spread about 0.43), so P(exceed) is about 37.5%. Multiplied by about 95% that bidding concludes by end-2028, that gives about 36%. A SpaceX bidding war is the main route above the threshold. Third-tranche diminishing returns and $16B of add-on costs are the main reasons it falls short.

SpaceX filed in the proceeding, asking the FCC to reserve part of the band for D2D and to let satellite coverage satisfy buildout. The FCC rebuffed both, which weakens SpaceX's case but signals interest, and analysts expect it to bid ('Elon is coming'). It qualified and won small licences in Auction 113, bidding in only six markets, which may have been practice. I estimate about 60-65% that it applies and about 70% that it wins at least one of 3,248 PEA licences if it bids seriously. The deduction is for terrestrial-only buildout obligations and Musk's 'last piece' comment.

The FCC approved the transfer on 12 May 2026, the licences have been in trust since 22 May, and closing is targeted for 30 Nov 2027. That is a high-probability event with only about one month of slack before the deadline. The risks are slippage past 31 Dec, claims from the Dish DBS and Dish Wireless Chapter 11 estates, and SpaceX share-price or financing issues. I come out a little below the research's 85%.

The FCC accepted the filing in Nov 2026, with petitions due around 1-8 Dec. On the usual 180-day informal shot clock, a decision would come around mid-2027, leaving about six months of buffer. Every major spectrum transfer in 2025-26 was approved, often with conditions, including T-Mobile-Grain for the same licences and the approval of SpaceX-EchoStar in about eight months. A new entrant adding low-band is pro-competitive, which counters Carr's over-consolidation remark. The main risks are public-safety interference concerns about satellite use of 800 MHz and political volatility.

EchoStar's AWS-4, H-block and AWS-3 close around Nov 2027, which leaves about 13 months, and Grain's 800 MHz closes around mid-2027. Next-generation D2D satellites launch from 2027, with expanded service targeted for end-2027. Shotwell says SpaceX wants to be a full mobile telco, and a Starlink-billed satellite or hybrid plan for broadband subscribers would satisfy the resolution. Against that: slips in the Starship launch cadence, handset band support, the carriers refusing wholesale access, and SpaceX's history of missing timelines. I match the research's 55%.

The bar is the larger cable operator, probably about 22-30M lines by 2035, because AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile stay far ahead. My 2030 SpaceX distribution (median 1.8M, P90 9M) implies only about a 10-15% chance of passing 25M directly billed lines by 2035. Paths to it include an acquisition of a subscriber base or a cheap satellite plan that scales. The new-entrant record (DISH, Clearwire) argues for caution.

SpaceX needs about 80,000 sites and wants subscribers. Small regional facilities-based carriers (C Spire, Cellcom and others), Boost (arguably) and the cable companies' mobile businesses are all buyable targets that would count, and SpaceX has a stock currency of about $1.9T. Amazon's purchase of Globalstar shows hyperscaler appetite. Against that: these acquirers have historically built rather than bought carriers, regulators and Deutsche Telekom stand in the way of any large deal, and the research gives about 20% to its 2030 'convergence premium' scenario.

For revenue per GB to rise in a year, traffic growth would have to fall below revenue growth of about 2-4%. Even my P10 traffic path (about 10.5% CAGR) keeps yearly growth well above that. The probability comes mainly from a CTIA methodology break or restatement, as with the 2015 and 2017 survey anomalies, or a sharp FWA rationing shock. The research gives about 20% to a broader 'crunch' that includes capex intensity, but this question is narrower.

US growth decelerated from 38% to 20% between 2022 and 2025, and my median path continues down to 12% by 2030. On the other side, Ericsson's Q2 2026 global re-acceleration to 23% was led by North America, upper C-band capacity could revive FWA, and AI uplink is a wildcard. There are four annual draws, and the CTIA series is lumpy. The research estimates about 15%, and I tilt slightly up for the bull factors.

The Rel-21 ASN.1 freeze is in March 2029. US carriers launched 5G about 9-13 months after the Rel-15 ASN.1 freeze, which points to late 2029 or 2030. T-Mobile says it will be 'first with 6G in this country', Qualcomm targets commercial 6G systems from 2029, and an AT&T engineer expects 'a little cluster of 6G to make a marketing claim' in 2030, which would count. The risks are 3GPP slippage, chipset readiness, weak ROI and flat capex, with 7 GHz spectrum probably not yet in place.

2.7 GHz (about 210 MHz, below 4.2 GHz) probably fills the first statutory federal tranche (identify by July 2027, auction by July 2029). That pushes 7.125-7.4 GHz and 4.4-4.94 GHz into the second tranche, due for auction by July 2033. A 2030 auction would need NTIA's Dec 2026 study to come back favourable, an FCC rulemaking in 2027-28 and no Defense Department or fixed-link holdouts. The 6G push and WRC-27 (in force from 2029) help, but US mid-band auctions usually slip 1-3 years.

EchoStar told the FCC it would sell its remaining 700 MHz, paired AWS-3, CBRS, C-band and other licences by 1 Sept 2028, as a condition of its waivers. Its paired AWS-3 is marked at about $8.1B and Verizon has been interested, so P(definitive agreement by end-2028) is about 75% on its own. Add Array's C-band (about 40%), Anterix's strategic review after it raised its value estimate to $2.5-7B (about 25%) and NextNav (about 10%), and the chance of at least one is high. The deduction allows for correlated failure (a buyer strike after Auction 115) and for doubt over whether a partial sale counts as 'most'.

Over most 4-year windows since 2010, US telcos have lagged the S&P 500 (a base rate of roughly 30-35%). Today they start from depressed valuations after the 9 Oct selloff (T-Mobile down about 22% year to date) with 4-6% dividend yields, while the S&P carries AI-boom valuations, which helps the relative case. The spectrum thesis does not clearly help the incumbents, because markets treat SpaceX's spectrum as a competitive negative. I give a slight uplift to the research's 35%.

Starting points: the 2021 lower C-band ($0.945), 3.45 GHz ($0.70) and TD Cowen's $30-75B range ($0.56-1.40). The 2021 price was set when Verizon and AT&T had almost no mid-band. They now hold 160-200+ MHz of C-band and 3.45 GHz, AT&T is at 3.1x leverage after paying $23B for EchoStar, and T-Mobile says it will bid only if spectrum is cheaper than densifying. Winners also carry about $16B of clearing and altimeter costs, and abroad, second tranches of similar bands clear lower (Canada 3800 MHz came in about 90% below 3500 MHz). The upper tail stays fat because a block next to the incumbents' C-band is worth a lot to them, and SpaceX could bid. I put P(>$0.94 | concludes) at about 29%.

This is the price distribution times 53.6B MHz-pops (160 MHz x 335M), so the two stay consistent. My median of about $41B sits below the midpoint of the analyst ranges (TD Cowen $30-75B, Carr $30-60B) and below the $81B of 2021, for the reasons in the price rationale. US auctions have missed consensus badly in both directions (AWS-3 and C-band well above, 600 MHz and 2.5 GHz well below), hence the wide range.

By my count, the median of the 2025-26 deals above $1B is about $1.20. Most of that wave came from EchoStar's forced exit and SpaceX's one-off build-out. In 2029-30 the observations are more likely to be FCC auctions of 2.7 GHz, 1675/2020 MHz or 4.4 GHz, which carry federal exclusion zones and large supply and should clear around $0.3-0.7. Private low-band sales, if any, would come in around $1.2-2.0. Which deals happen drives the result, so the range is wide, centred below today's median.

From 2013 to 2024 the base rate was about 0.2 deals of $5B+ a year. 2025-26 produced 3, almost all from EchoStar's FCC-forced exit, and SpaceX says its portfolio is now complete. The most likely $5B+ deal in the window is EchoStar's remaining paired AWS-3 (New Street values it at about $8.1B), though it could be split into smaller pieces or signed before January 2027. Beyond that, few nationwide holdings outside the big three are left to sell. I model this as Poisson-like with mean about 1.0 and some overdispersion: P(0) about 38%.

CTIA counted 159.3 EB in 2025 after growth fell from 32% to 20%. Mature-market analogues (UK +18%, Switzerland 20-25% and falling) and Ericsson's 13% per-smartphone CAGR, which has historically run high, point to growth fading to about 10-14% by 2030. FWA, the main driver, is slowing (Verizon added 159K vs 261K), and 82-89% of smartphone data rides Wi-Fi. My P50 path is roughly +18, +15, +13, +12 and +11% for 2026-30 (about 13.5% CAGR). Ericsson's mid-2026 note that North America is leading global growth keeps the upper tail open.

I extend the 2030 distribution at about 7-12% a year for 2031-35, the decay seen in every maturing market and in Ericsson's own forecast (14% by 2031). The log-scale upper tail allows for AI and physical-AI uplink scenarios (Nokia's 44% AI share of all network traffic by 2035), but vendor forecasts from Ericsson, Nokia and CTIA have consistently overshot. CTIA's own 4x-by-2032 path sits near my P90.

The only measurement is 0.06% (Ericsson, April 2025), and none has appeared since. Reaching even 1.5% by 2030 means AI traffic growing roughly 2.2x a year in absolute terms while total traffic doubles. Text AI is light, a lot of inference is moving on-device or server-to-server, and glasses and indoor robots ride Wi-Fi or the phone. The log-wide upper tail reflects multimodal voice and camera assistants, AI video apps, and vendors' incentive to define 'AI traffic' broadly when they publish the 'best measurement'.

About 19M now. Industry adds are decaying from 3.8M (2025) to about 3.6M (2026), and I assume roughly 2.8, 2.3, 1.9 and 1.5M for 2027-30, as disconnects rise and AT&T and Verizon prioritise fiber. By carrier at end-2030 that is roughly T-Mobile 14-15M (near its 15M target), Verizon about 9M and AT&T 4.5-5.5M. Upper C-band capacity from 2028-30 supports the upside, against New Street's estimated ~32M ceiling.

This is my service-revenue P50 ($262B) divided by my traffic P50 (300 EB), with roughly independent uncertainty in each. The historical -20% a year came from 25-35% traffic growth. With traffic slowing to about 13% and revenue growing about 2.3%, the decline slows to about -10% a year. The ratio's spread is mostly traffic uncertainty.

The outcomes cluster. Upper C-band 160 MHz is about 96% likely by 2030. 1675/2020 MHz (25 MHz) is about 60%, with its NPRM in October 2026. 2.7 GHz (about 210 MHz) is about 50%: Carr targets 2028 and the statutory federal deadline is July 2029, but US mid-band auctions have slipped 1-3 years. 7.125-7.4 GHz or part of 4.4-4.94 GHz is about 30% combined. That puts about 35% of the mass at 160-185 MHz, about 35% at 370-395 MHz and the rest above 430 MHz.

The 2025 law requires 300 MHz from the FCC plus 500 MHz of federal spectrum. But the easiest federal bands (3.1-3.45 and 7.4-8.4 GHz, 1,350 MHz) are excluded, the Defense Department prefers sharing to clearing, and the FCC's auction authority lapses in September 2034. About 75% of the 2012 Spectrum Act targets were met within the decade, which supports a P50 near 600 rather than the full 800 MHz. The P90 allows for a WRC-27-driven 7 GHz or 15 GHz tranche.

The base case is 79 MHz: EchoStar's AWS-4, H-block and unpaired AWS-3 (65 MHz, FCC-approved, about 95% likely to close by 2030) plus Grain's 800 MHz (14 MHz, about 88% likely). The P10 is the case where the Grain deal fails. Upside comes from Auction 115 wins (about 47% chance of any win, probably small nationwide-equivalent amounts) and a possible purchase of EchoStar's paired AWS-3. Musk called the 800 MHz deal the 'last critical piece', which caps the median.

Revenue today is well under $1B: SpaceX does not disclose its figure and AST's $150-200M guidance is mostly non-subscriber. The whole legacy satellite-phone (MSS) industry earns a few $B a year. D2D is mostly bundled into carrier plans at near-zero marginal price, and SpaceX, AST, Amazon and Apple/Globalstar will all be competing. Next-generation capacity from 2027-28 and 22M+ monthly users support growth of about 1.6-2x a year from about $0.4B. My median is below the brief's $6B.

SpaceX now guides to a US Starlink Mobile service on its own spectrum in early 2028. I give about 80% to some directly billed plan by end-2030, leaving about 20% at zero. If it launches, about three years in market at the pace of Dish/Boost (about 7M, mostly acquired) or the cable MVNOs (about 24M in 8 years, with bundles and free lines) suggests a median of about 1.5M with a wide range. SpaceX has 79 MHz against T-Mobile's about 400 MHz, so urban capacity limits it.

Revenue was $235B in 2025 and has grown about 3% a year nominal since 2007. The 2026 mix is +5-6% at AT&T and T-Mobile against ARPA -1.9% at Verizon, with cable free lines and SpaceX entry pressuring price. FWA revenue adds about 0.5 points a year. I use about 2.2% CAGR. The CTIA-basis figure itself is uncertain (other trackers show $255-326B), which widens the range a little.

The multiple is about 6.9x today, and the US incumbents have traded in a 6-8x band. I lean slightly lower: SpaceX and cable competition, a 6G and upper C-band capex cycle around 2030, and markets punishing every SpaceX spectrum step (-9 to -13% on 9 October 2026). The brief's scenario weights are 50% grind (6-7.5x), 30% price pressure (5-6x) and 20% convergence premium (8x+). I shade the premium case down slightly.

24.1M in Q3 2026, adding about 3.4M a year, but Comcast adds are slowing (368K vs 414K) and both broadband bases are shrinking, which caps attach rates. Decaying adds of about 2.8, 2.4, 2.0 and 1.6M for 2027-30 on an end-2026 base of about 25M give about 34M. The P90 is linear continuation helped by Cox's footprint. The P10 adds free-line roll-off churn and SpaceX competition.

Capex has been flat at $29-30B for 2023-25. Verizon trimmed its 2026 guide, AT&T cut its long-term outlook and T-Mobile is at about $10B. Upper C-band deployment in 2028-30 and early 6G add some spend in 2030. Inflation adds a little nominal growth, but carriers are in harvest mode and no capacity crunch is visible. A return to the $39B peak needs a 2018-22-style cycle, which sits in my upper tail.

Rules are final, bidding starts 27 April 2027, and the statute requires the auction by July 2027. Recent clock-plus-assignment auctions took about 10-13 weeks (Auction 107 Dec-Feb, Auction 110 Oct-Jan), so even a start delayed by a quarter or a long clock phase still closes in 2027. The residual risk is litigation, shutdowns or procedural slips.

P(bidding concludes by 2028) is about 0.94, and P(price > $0.94 | concludes) is about 0.29 from my price distribution (P50 $0.76, P90 $1.25). The incumbents' mid-band needs are much smaller than in 2021, and balance sheets are stretched after EchoStar. Clearing costs and the large 160 MHz block push the price below the 2021 level, so only a SpaceX bidding war or an adjacency fight gets it above.

For: SpaceX qualified for and won licences in Auction 113 (only $8.5M), says it wants to be a full mobile telco, is seeking 80,000 sites and has IPO cash. Against: the FCC refused satellite buildout credit, so licences carry terrestrial obligations; Musk called 800 MHz the last piece needed; and capital competes with AI. A token rural win counts, which keeps this near a coin flip.

The FCC approved the transfer in May 2026 and the licences are in trust, so the main remaining question is timing. The contractual target is 30 November 2027, leaving one month of buffer before the deadline. Risks are slippage, disputes from the bankruptcies of EchoStar's subsidiaries Dish DBS and Dish Wireless, and either party preferring to delay the cash payment. Both sides have strong incentives to close, and an earlier close is possible.

The FCC accepted the filing on 10 November 2026 with pleadings due in December, so the informal 180-day clock points to mid-2027. SpaceX holds no sub-1 GHz spectrum, so screen concerns are minimal, and T-Mobile shares in Grain's gain rather than opposing. Carr's FCC approved every major 2025-26 transfer. The residual risk is conditions-driven delay or Musk-related politics.

SpaceX now targets early 2028 for a Starlink Mobile service on its own spectrum, after the EchoStar closing (about 82% by end-2027, about 92% by end-2028). Dish's band n70 (AWS-4/H downlink, AWS-3 uplink) is already supported in phones, which eases a terrestrial or hybrid launch. Next-generation D2D satellites depend on Starship's launch cadence, and Musk-era timelines often slip a year. A one-year buffer gives about 60%.

SpaceX would need to pass the larger cable operator, Charter, likely 20-25M lines by 2035, with direct subscribers from a 2028 start. Dish never scaled despite plenty of spectrum, and cable took about 8 years to reach 24M with bundles and free lines on Verizon's network. Satellite-only cheap lines or buying a carrier are the main upside routes.

SpaceX's stated approach is to buy spectrum and build, not buy a telco (Light Reading). The big three are huge, and T-Mobile is controlled by Deutsche Telekom. Cable mobile is bundled with broadband. The plausible route is a small regional facilities-based carrier or a cable mobile carve-out for SpaceX or Amazon, which the brief's 20% 'convergence premium' state partly covers.

Revenue per GB has fallen every year since 2010 (-20% a year recently). A rise needs traffic growth below the roughly 2-3% revenue growth, which would take a traffic stall or a CTIA methodology change. Carriers are trimming capex and cutting real prices, which argues against scarcity pricing. The residual probability is mostly data and definition risk.

US growth decelerated from 38% to 20% between 2022 and 2025, and mature markets settle in the high teens. A year above 25% would need a new driver: an AI or uplink surge, cheap FWA on new C-band capacity, or a CTIA methodology jump like the 2015 and 2017 anomalies. Ericsson's mid-2026 'North America leading' growth note keeps this from being negligible. The brief puts it at 15%; I shade slightly lower.

Rel-21 ASN.1 freeze is March 2029. Matching LTE's 21 months from freeze to launch lands exactly at December 2030, while 5G's faster pace would make it comfortable. US policy and marketing races argue for a token paid launch, possibly FWA. Harvest-mode economics, no new 7 GHz spectrum yet, device availability and any 3GPP slip argue against.

NTIA's 7.125-7.4 GHz study is due December 2026, and the 2.7 GHz band alone can meet the July 2029 federal auction requirement, so 7 GHz is not forced by 2030. Identification-to-auction has taken 1.5-3 years (3.45 GHz was fast), and WRC-27 decisions take effect in 2029. I give about 22% to 7 GHz and about 12% to a 4.4-4.94 GHz slice, about 30% combined, matching the upper tail of my 2030 MHz forecast.

EchoStar told the FCC it would sell its remaining terrestrial licences by September 2028, it is a motivated forced seller, and New Street marks its paired AWS-3 at about $8.1B, which Verizon has discussed. That alone gives about 65%. Array's retained C-band, an Anterix sale or exit, and NextNav add some independent chance. The few buyers and Auction 115 as substitute supply keep this from being near-certain.

US telcos have underperformed the S&P 500 in most multi-year windows since 2010, and every SpaceX spectrum step has de-rated them. Against that, a starting point of about 6.9x EV/EBITDA, high FCF and dividend yields, and an AI-concentrated, richly valued S&P mean a defensive basket wins if the AI trade unwinds. About 4 years of tracking error makes this a little better than 1 in 3.

Price is my proceeds distribution divided by 53.6B MHz-pops (160 MHz x 335M). On this basis lower C-band was about $0.87, not $0.94. Winners also owe about $16B in add-on costs (incentive payments, clearing, altimeter rebates), about $0.30/MHz-pop or double the lower C-band's per-MHz burden. Each carrier already holds about 150 MHz or more of mid-band TDD, Verizon cites a 4-5 year deployment lag, AT&T is at 3.13x leverage after EchoStar, and 2.7 GHz follows in 2028. With 8 blocks per PEA and only three carriers, demand could roughly equal supply and clear near the 3.45 GHz level (~$0.67). A serious SpaceX bid (about 40%) is the main upside, and US mid-band auctions have often beaten consensus.

I treat this as a mixture. Without a serious fourth bidder (about 60%), proceeds center near $29B, as three carriers cut demand to fit 8 blocks per market. With SpaceX bidding seriously (about 40%), they center near $50B. The median sits below TD Cowen's $30-75B midpoint and Carr's $30-60B because of the ~$16B add-on costs and carrier restraint. The P90 stays high because lower C-band beat forecasts by 55-100%. Conditional on bidding concluding, which I put at about 96.5% by end-2028.

The 2029-30 deal set will probably be small (2-4 transactions). It mixes TDD mid-band auctions (2.7 GHz if it slips from 2028, 1675/2020 MHz, possibly part of 4.4 GHz) likely at $0.3-0.8, with private sales of paired or low-band spectrum (EchoStar leftovers, Anterix, SpaceX deals) at $1-2.5. By then upper C-band and 2.7 GHz add supply, so generic mid-band compresses while low-band keeps a premium. The median depends heavily on deal mix, hence the wide range.

The most likely $5B+ deal is EchoStar's paired AWS-3 (valued at $8-10B). EchoStar has committed to sell its remaining licences by September 2028 in exchange for buildout waivers, and Verizon has held talks. It may still be split into sub-$5B pieces. Other candidates are further SpaceX or Amazon purchases. The base rate was about 0.2 per year in 2013-24 and 3 in 2025-26, so I use roughly Poisson with a mean of 1.25 plus overdispersion.

Starting from 159.3 EB (+20% in 2025), I assume growth slows from about 17% in 2026 to about 12% in 2030. This follows Ericsson's 13% per-smartphone CAGR for North America, slowing FWA net adds, and mature markets settling near 20% or lower. The P10 assumes faster saturation (about 8-10% by 2029-30). The P90 assumes growth holds near 22%, CTIA's own 4x-by-2032 path. CTIA's series has methodology jumps, which widens both tails.

I extend the 2030 distribution at about 10% a year average growth for 2031-35 (Ericsson sees 14% globally by 2031 and falling). The low end assumes 6% from a weak 2030. The high end assumes AI or uplink-heavy devices and 6G/7 GHz FWA keep growth near 15-18%. The range is log-wide because five more years of compounding uncertainty sit on top of the 2030 range.

Measured GenAI traffic was 0.06% in April 2025. If AI-app traffic grows about 2.2x a year faster than total traffic, the 2030 share is about 3%. Ratios of 1.8x and 2.8x give about 1% and about 10%. The best measurement will probably come from vendors (Ericsson, Nokia) with an incentive toward broad inclusion of glasses, vehicles and agents, which fattens the upper tail. Wi-Fi offload and on-device inference cap the base case.

From about 19M in Q3 2026 (about 20M by end-2026), I let industry adds decay from about 3.6M in 2026 to about 1.5-2M by 2030. That fits Verizon's slowing adds and AT&T's fiber priority, and is offset by T-Mobile's 15M target and AT&T's EchoStar 3.45 GHz enabling more Internet Air. New Street's ~32M Big-3 capacity estimate bounds the P90. T-Mobile no longer discloses its count, which adds measurement noise.

This is the ratio of my service-revenue P50 ($267B) to my traffic P50 (312 EB). Revenue varies far less than traffic, so the range is close to the inverse of the traffic distribution. It implies about -10% a year, a slower decline than 2020-25's -20%, because traffic growth is slowing.

Upper C-band contributes 160 MHz (about 97%) and is a point mass that sets the P10. 2.7 GHz adds about 200 MHz with roughly 70% odds by 2030: relocation plans were approved in April 2026, Carr targets 2028, and the statute requires 200 MHz of federal spectrum auctioned by July 2029. 1675/2020 MHz adds about 25 MHz (about 50%). Upper mid-band (7.125-7.4 GHz or 4.4 GHz) adds about 275-400 MHz at about 30%, and a mmWave auction is a small tail. FCC and NTIA timelines typically slip 1-3 years, and once 300 MHz is auctioned the statute stops forcing more.

By 2035, upper C-band and 2.7 GHz are very likely (about 360 MHz combined). 7.125-7.4 GHz (275 MHz) is about 60% after the WRC-27 identification and the statutory 2033 tranche. 4.4 GHz (up to 400 MHz) is about 40-45%: study plans were cleared in July 2026, but DoD and DOJ are major users. The Spectrum Act precedent delivered about 75% of its targets within a decade. DoD resistance and the exclusion of 3.1-3.45 and 7.4-8.4 GHz cap the upside.

The base is about 79 MHz: EchoStar's 65 MHz (closing is about 85% by end-2027 and about 93% by 2030) plus Grain's 2x7 MHz (about 90% approved). Small AWS-3 and Tristar holdings add little. Upside comes from Auction 115 wins (about 52% to win anything, about 38% for a meaningful 20-80 MHz nationwide-equivalent), EchoStar's paired AWS-3, and 2.7 GHz. SpaceX added about 79 MHz in 13 months and wants terrestrial capacity, but it is spending about $20B a quarter on capex, mostly for AI.

Revenue is well under $1B in 2026. SpaceX's V2 constellation (service on its own spectrum targeted for early 2028), AST's 2027-28 ramp and Amazon's 2028 entry could take wholesale plus retail to a few billion dollars. For example, 100-200M Starlink Mobile users at $0.5-2 a month wholesale is $0.6-4.8B, plus AST, IoT and Apple-linked revenue. Bundling at near-zero prices and Starship or launch slips pull it down. Legacy MSS (a few $B in total) is the scale anchor.

SpaceX guided on its Q3 call to switch on Starlink Mobile on its own spectrum in early 2028. Musk's timelines usually slip, and T-Mobile refuses an MVNO, so urban indoor coverage would depend on SpaceX's own sites (80,000-site talks, possibly Dish base stations). There is about a 30% chance of essentially zero direct-billed subscribers at end-2030. Conditional on launch the median is about 1.5M, with upside from Starlink broadband bundling or buying Boost's base. Dish/Boost and the cable MVNOs show that entrants scale slowly.

Starting from $235B in 2025, I assume about +4% in 2026 (AT&T wireless service +5%, T-Mobile +6%, price increases, FWA) and about 2.5% a year after that, close to the ~3% nominal CAGR since 2007. The 2025 base of $235B is unverified; other trackers give $255-326B. The P10 is a price-pressure path (SpaceX plus cable free lines, flat nominal from 2027). The P90 assumes rational three-network pricing after the EchoStar exit, plus FWA and IoT growth. The range is widened for uncertainty about how CTIA defines the series.

The carriers have historically traded at 6-8x EV/EBITDA. T-Mobile's 7.4x is unusually low after the SpaceX shock, so partial mean reversion is plausible if SpaceX's terrestrial build proves slow. On the downside, an upper C-band and 6G capex cycle around 2030 plus SpaceX and cable price pressure could push the average to 5.5-6x. Spectrum M&A or a re-rating takes it above 8x.

The base is 24.1M in Q3 2026, adding about 3.4M a year with Comcast's adds already decaying (368k vs 414k). Linear extrapolation gives about 38.6M and a 10-20% annual decay in adds gives 33-36M. Penetration of the cable broadband base is still low (about 14-25%), but shrinking broadband subscriber counts, free-line roll-off and possible SpaceX competition cap the upside.

Capex has been flat at $29-30B nominal for 2023-25, and Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile are all guiding flat or down (harvest mode, fiber priority). 2030 sits at the turn toward an upper C-band, 2.7 GHz and early-6G deployment cycle, but Verizon's 4-5 year deployment lag and altimeter retrofits push the heavy spend toward 2031-32. A 5G-style surge (+42% to the 2022 peak) is the P90 tail. SpaceX's own build probably falls outside the CTIA basis.

Bidding starts on 27 April 2027 and the statute requires the auction by July 2027. Clock-plus-assignment auctions of this size (Auctions 107 and 110) took about 10-13 weeks, so a start slip of up to about 5 months still closes in 2027. Auctions continued through past shutdowns, and courts rarely stay them. The residual risk is litigation or a postponement over the cable-video or altimeter transition.

Clearing above $0.94 on the question's 335M-pop basis means gross bids above $50.4B, more than lower C-band's own ~$0.87 on that basis. That sits at about the 73rd percentile of my proceeds distribution (P50 $37B, P90 $70B), so about 26.7% conditional, times about 96.5% that bidding concludes by end-2028. Reaching it essentially requires SpaceX to bid seriously against Verizon.

SpaceX qualified for and won licences in the 2026 AWS-3 re-auction, took part in the upper C-band rulemaking, and is reported to be expected to bid. Analysts expect an aggressive bid. With 3,248 PEA licences it can win rural blocks cheaply if it enters. On the other side, the FCC refused satellite-coverage buildout credit, SpaceX's capex is going mainly to AI, and Musk called the 800 MHz deal the last critical piece. I put about 72% on applying and about 72% on winning given an application.

The FCC approved the transfer in May 2026 and the licences sit in a trust. The closing is contractually targeted for 30 November 2027, which aligns with SpaceX funding interest through that date and its guidance for service on its own spectrum in early 2028. Both parties have strong incentives to close. The risks are only one month of slack before the deadline, the Dish subsidiaries' Chapter 11 cases, and possible creditor litigation.

The FCC accepted the filing on 10 November 2026 (petitions due 1 December, oppositions 8 December). The informal 180-day review points to about May-June 2027, and the deadline leaves 13 months. This FCC approved every major 2025-26 transfer, including SpaceX-EchoStar in about 8 months and T-Mobile-Grain quickly. SpaceX holds no low-band, so the below-1-GHz screen does not bind. The residual risks are 800 MHz public-safety interference objections, conditions-related delay, and a Musk-administration falling-out.

SpaceX's Q3 2026 guidance is to switch on Starlink Mobile on its own spectrum in early 2028, after the November 2027 EchoStar closing (about 85%). Many phones already support Dish's band 70/66 frequencies. That leaves about 12 months of buffer against Musk's usual slips: T-Mobile's satellite service moved roughly 1.5-2 years from announcement to commercial launch, and V2 satellites depend on Starship cadence. I estimate about 93% that the closing happens by end-2028 and about 60% that a paid SpaceX-billed plan launches in time given closing.

The fourth-largest operator in 2035 will almost certainly be Charter or Comcast, likely at 22-30M lines, so SpaceX would need 25M or more directly billed US subscribers. US entrants (Dish/Boost, the cable MVNOs) took 5-8 years to reach single-digit to roughly 20M, and with help from incumbents' networks. Without an MVNO host, SpaceX's satellite capacity cannot serve dense indoor demand. The probability rests mainly on a large acquisition or a hugely successful cheap satellite-only plan.

Several plausible paths exist: SpaceX buying a regional facilities-based carrier for sites, operations and customers to support its terrestrial build, a Boost-type base (borderline under the resolution), or Amazon extending Leo and Globalstar into mobile. Big-3 or cable mobile-unit takeovers are very unlikely, since the cable mobile businesses exist to defend the broadband bundle. SpaceX's AI capex competes for the capital. The 2025-26 tech deals bought spectrum and satellite operators, not carriers.

Revenue per GB rises only if traffic grows more slowly than revenue (about 2-4%) in some year. Even my slowest traffic path keeps growth at 8% or more through 2030. The main route to Yes is a CTIA survey or methodology break (the series has anomalies in 2015-18) or carriers throttling FWA hard.

Growth fell from 32% to 20% in 2025, FWA adds are slowing, and Ericsson projects decelerating growth. Getting above 25% would need a new driver (AI uplink devices, cheap FWA on newly cleared spectrum) or a CTIA methodology jump like the 2018 spike. Four annual chances keep the probability above negligible. This is slightly below the research team's 15%.

The Release 21 ASN.1 freeze is March 2029. The first US 5G launch came about 10 months after its freeze and LTE about 21, so end-2030 sits at the slow end of the range. T-Mobile says it intends to be first in the US with 6G around 2030, Ericsson expects first commercial systems in 2030, and the US-China race politics resemble 2019, all pointing to a token launch, possibly on existing or upper C-band spectrum. Harvest-mode capex, no 7 GHz spectrum by 2030 and chipset timing pull the other way.

NTIA's 7.125-7.4 GHz report is due 10 December 2026 and WRC-27 decides in November 2027. 4.4 GHz study plans were cleared in July 2026 (up to 400 MHz) and the administration has sped up the relocation process. The fast 3.45 GHz precedent took about 17 months from identification to auction. But 2.7 GHz alone can meet the statute's 2029 federal tranche, which removes forcing for upper mid-band until 2033. DoD resistance and the 1-3 year slips typical of NTIA and FCC timelines make concluding bidding by end-2030 less likely than not.

EchoStar has told the FCC it will sell its remaining terrestrial licences by September 2028 in exchange for buildout waivers. Its paired AWS-3 (valued at $8-10B) has an obvious buyer in Verizon, which took 88% of Auction 113, and SpaceX is a second possible bidder. I give EchoStar alone about 72%. Array's retained C-band (about 35%), Anterix (about 20%) and NextNav (about 10%) add independent chances, though only four or five buyers exist.

Over 4-year windows since 2010, the carrier basket has usually lagged the tech-led S&P 500; only T-Mobile beat it consistently. The base rate is roughly 25-30%. Today's depressed multiples (about 6.9x after the SpaceX shock), a basket dividend yield near 4% against about 1.2% for the S&P, and S&P valuation risk from the AI boom raise the odds somewhat. SpaceX execution and an upper C-band/6G capex cycle around 2030 are headwinds.
